title: Whitewashed Walls and False Prophets
summary: God speaks through Ezekiel against the prophets of Israel who invent their messages, promise peace when there is no peace, and cover a flimsy wall with whitewash instead of repairing it. The storm of judgment will bring the wall down and expose them. God then condemns women who prophesy falsely and use magic bands and veils to trap people for handfuls of barley, and he promises to free his people from their hands.
story: Chapter 12 ended by answering the popular sayings that dismissed prophecy. Chapter 13 turns to the people who made those sayings plausible: the prophets who told Jerusalem and the exiles that all would be well. Ezekiel's struggle is not only with unbelief but with rival voices claiming to speak for the same God. The chapter belongs to the long section of chapters 12 to 24, which strips away every false support the people leaned on before Jerusalem fell. Chapter 14 continues the theme, addressing the elders who come to a prophet while keeping idols in their hearts.
historical:
Ezekiel's contemporary Jeremiah faced the same problem in Jerusalem during the same years. He records prophets who said “Peace, peace” when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 8:11), and a confrontation with the prophet Hananiah, who promised in 594 or 593 BC that the exiles and temple vessels would return within two years (Jeremiah 28). Jeremiah also wrote to the exiles in Babylon, warning them against prophets among them, and named two, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah (Jeremiah 29:21-23). Ezekiel's oracle does not name individuals, but it describes the same kind of voices at work among the exiles.

The standard for testing a prophet came from Deuteronomy 18:21-22: a word that does not come to pass was not spoken by the LORD. Ezekiel's opponents were betting on a future that would prove them wrong within a few years, when Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC.
cultural:
Two images from building would have been clear to any ancient listener. Walls in the region were often built of stone or mud brick and plastered with a lime wash or clay coating. A thin coat of whitewash could make a poorly built wall look sound, but a heavy rainstorm would wash the plaster off and bring down a wall whose structure was weak. The prophets' job was to stand in the gaps and repair the wall (verse 5), meaning to call the people to repentance and intercede for them. Instead they plastered over the cracks with reassuring words. The image of foxes among ruins (verse 4) suggests scavengers who make their dens in the rubble and profit from the damage rather than repairing it.

The women condemned in verses 17 to 23 appear to have practiced a form of divination or magic. The exact meaning of the objects is uncertain. The “magic charms” sewn on wrists and the “veils” for people's heads were probably amulets and coverings used in rituals to bind or control, a practice known from Mesopotamian magic, where knotting and binding were common. The women were paid in barley and bread, suggesting that they served ordinary people for small fees. Israel had true women prophets, including Miriam, Deborah, and Huldah, so the charge here is not that they were women but that they used false words and magic to manipulate life and death.
literary: The chapter has two parallel oracles: against male prophets (verses 1 to 16) and against female prophets (verses 17 to 23). Both open with the command to prophesy against those who speak “out of their own imagination” (verses 2 and 17), both pronounce a woe (verses 3 and 18), and both close with the recognition formula. The first oracle develops the image of the wall in steps: the prophets did not repair it (verse 5), they whitewashed it (verse 10), God will bring a storm (verses 11 to 13), and the wall will fall and expose its foundation (verse 14). The second oracle develops the image of trapping birds, with God as the one who tears the snares away and lets the birds go free (verse 20).

outline.t: Prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing
The whitewashed wall and the coming storm
Women who ensnare souls with charms and veils
God frees his people like birds from a snare

doctrines.note: True prophecy comes from God, not from human imagination or wishful thinking. The chapter draws a sharp line between those God sends and those who say “Thus declares the LORD” when he has not spoken (verse 7).

False prophets will be excluded from the council of God's people and from the register of Israel (verse 9). Those who mislead others about God bear a heavy responsibility, and judgment will expose their work for what it is.

The women's magic is a form of idolatry: trying to control life and death through ritual power rather than trusting God. It profanes God's name among his people (verse 19) by treating him as a force to be manipulated.

words.note: Shalom, peace. It means far more than the absence of war: wholeness, safety, and well-being. The false prophets promised shalom to a city facing destruction (verses 10 and 16). Their message was not wrong in hoping for peace but in announcing it where God had not given it.

Tafel, whitewash. The word describes a coating or plaster, and elsewhere a related word means something tasteless or unseasoned. The false prophets' message was a cosmetic coat over a failing structure, a way of making things look sound without making them sound.

Navi, prophet. A prophet was someone who spoke on God's behalf. The same title belongs to Ezekiel and to his opponents, which is exactly the problem: the title alone did not show who was sent by God. The test was faithfulness to God's word and its fulfillment.

Nefesh, soul, life, or person. It appears eight times in verses 18 to 20. It does not mean an immaterial soul in the later philosophical sense but the whole living person. The women were said to hunt persons, and God promises to set those persons free.

christ: Jesus warned against false prophets who come in sheep's clothing (Matthew 7:15) and against those who would claim his name while misleading many (Matthew 24:11, 24). He also rebuked religious leaders as whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of death within (Matthew 23:27), an image that echoes the whitewashed wall of this chapter. The chapter's hope, that God himself will tear away the snares and free his people, is fulfilled in the one whom the New Testament calls the true Word of God, who came to set the captives free (Luke 4:18). These links are thematic rather than predictive.

hard.q: How can anyone tell a true prophet from a false one, if both claim to speak for God?
hard.a: Ezekiel's audience faced exactly this problem, and the Old Testament gives several tests. Deuteronomy 18 says that a prophet whose word does not come to pass has not spoken from God, and Deuteronomy 13 says that even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he leads people after other gods. Ezekiel adds a moral test: false prophets comfort the wicked and discourage the righteous (verse 22), and they tell people what they want to hear. The New Testament continues along these lines, asking believers to test the spirits by their confession of Christ (1 John 4:1-3) and by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-20). None of these tests is instant; the exiles had to wait and see. But the pattern is clear: a true word calls people to God and to repentance, even when it is unwelcome.

questions: The false prophets whitewashed a weak wall instead of repairing it. Where are you tempted to cover a problem with reassuring words rather than face it?
Why are messages of peace and safety so appealing, even when they are untrue?
The prophets were supposed to stand in the gaps. Who in your life has done that for you, and for whom could you do it?
